blocks.text: Pisiform is a sesamoid bone located in the proximal row of the carpal bones but does not participate directly in the radiocarpal articulation.
Wrist joint
Synovial ellipsoidal (condyloid) joint allowing flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and circumduction.
Articulating Bones
The wrist joint involves the distal end of the radius and the proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum).
The ulna is not directly involved in the wrist joint but is adjacent to it, separated by an articular disc (the triangular fibrocartilage).
Carpal Bones Involved
Scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum are directly involved in the articulation with the radius. The pisiform is not involved in the wrist joint.
Joint Capsule
A fibrous joint capsule encloses the wrist joint, which is lined by a synovial membrane that produces synovial fluid for lubrication.
Ligaments
Movements
Blood Supply
The wrist joint is supplied by branches of the radial and ulnar arteries.
Nerve Supply
Clinical Relevance
Common conditions affecting the wrist joint include wrist fractures (especially of the scaphoid and radius), carpal tunnel syndrome, and arthritis.

The scenario describes a case of subclavian artery occlusion, in which the suprascapular artery (branch of subclavian artery) and the circumflex scapular artery (branch of axillary artery) form the most critical anastomosis for ensuring collateral blood flow to the upper limb.
Anastomosis of the Scapula
It is formed between the branches of the 1st part of the subclavian artery and the 3rd part of the axillary artery at the following two locations:

items.text: Around the body of the scapula
Suprascapular artery (branch of the thyrocervical trunk)
Circumflex scapular artery (branch of the subscapular artery from the 3rd part of the axillary artery)
Deep branch of the transverse cervical artery (branch of the thyrocervical trunk).
Acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery (2nd part of axillary).
Acromial branch of the suprascapular artery (1st part of subclavian).
Acromial branch of the posterior circumflex humeral artery (3rd part of axillary).

blocks.text: Collateral circulation through scapular anastomosis

The arterial anastomoses (scapular) provide collateral circulation through which blood can flow to the limb when the subclavian or axillary artery is blocked (anywhere between 1st part of the subclavian artery and 3rd part of axillary artery).
**Suprascapular artery and dorsal scapular artery (Option A):** are the branches of the thyrocervical trunk and transverse cervical artery, respectively; both are subclavian artery branches.
**Subscapular and circumflex scapular arteries (Option B):** are branches of the 3rd part of the axillary artery.
**Superior thoracic artery and acromiothoracic artery (Option C):** are axillary artery branches from the 1st and 2nd part, respectively.

The ulnar nerve supplies all the intrinsic muscles of the hand except the thenar muscles and lateral two lumbricals and is responsible for the sensations of the medial 11½ fingers of the hand. Hence abnormal sensations in the little finger and part of the ring finger with weakness on the palm side would be due to the ulnar nerve injury.
Damage to the ulnar nerve leads to:

items.text: Difficulty in flexing the fourth and fifth fingers due to paralysis of the flexor digitorum profundus (medial part) and the lumbricals (3rd and 4th).
Inability to adduct the thumb, as the adductor pollicis is also innervated by the ulnar nerve.

blocks.text: Ulnar nerve supply
**Radial nerve (Option B):** The radial nerve injury is characterised by wrist drop and does not cause the symptoms mentioned in this case.
**Median nerve (Option C):** the median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and is responsible for sensations on the medial side of the index finger, middle finger, and lateral side of the ring finger.
**Axillary nerve (Option D):** Responsible for the nerve supply of the deltoid muscle in the shoulder region.
